key_points: The most common cause of rectal bleeding in infants and toddlers — visible bright red blood on nappies or wipes, or crying during bowel movements
Cause in infants: almost always constipation — diet change (introduction of solids at 6 months); insufficient fibre; cow's milk-based formula (more constipating than breast milk); iron supplements

Diagnosis: inspect anal region with gentle buttock separation under adequate light — most paediatric fissures are posterior midline and visible without instrumentation; do NOT perform DRE in an infant with suspected fissure

Treatment in children and infants: dietary modification (high-fibre — pureed fruits, vegetables; adequate water/fluids); gentle warm baths (not sitz baths per se — simply bathe the perianal area gently in warm water); stool softeners (lactulose syrup for infants; macrogol sachets for toddlers); topical lidocaine gel for pain; usually resolves within 2-4 weeks
Surgical intervention rarely needed in children; botulinum toxin has been used in resistant cases

IMPORTANT safeguarding consideration: lateral anal fissures in children, multiple fissures, or fissures with bruising or unusual features may indicate sexual abuse — mandatory report to child protection services; careful sensitive examination and history; forensic medical examination if indicated

Common in both pregnancy (progesterone slows gut motility → constipation; iron supplements cause constipation) and post-partum (obstetric perineal trauma; post-delivery constipation from dehydration and reduced oral intake)
Diagnosis: clinical inspection as in non-pregnant women; avoid proctoscopy or DRE if possible due to discomfort

SAFE treatments in pregnancy: dietary fibre (Isabgol) — safe; warm sitz baths — safe; lactulose — safe; macrogol — safe; topical lidocaine — safe; topical diltiazem 2% cream (preferred over GTN for breastfeeding — less systemic absorption)

GTN: generally considered safe in pregnancy at topical doses but headache is poorly tolerated in post-partum women; systemic vasodilation theoretically reduces uterine blood flow in large doses — use with caution in pregnancy
AVOID: codeine-containing analgesics (constipating and cause neonatal respiratory depression); systemic NSAIDs in 3rd trimester; castor oil (stimulates uterine contractions)
Botulinum toxin: limited safety data in pregnancy — avoid; post-partum, Botox is acceptable; minimal to no excretion in breast milk

Surgical LIS: post-partum, if anal fissure persists beyond 3 months and is severe, LIS can be performed; take obstetric history carefully (sphincter integrity assessment before surgery — prior 3rd/4th degree tears increase incontinence risk from LIS)
Higher prevalence of secondary causes in elderly — biopsy any atypical fissure in patients >45-50 years to exclude anal SCC
Constipation is the predominant cause — polypharmacy (opioids, calcium channel blockers, diuretics — all constipating); reduced activity; reduced fluid intake; poor dietary diversity
Pre-existing sphincter weakness is common in elderly (reduced IAS and EAS tone with ageing — particularly after multiple childbirths in women) — increases incontinence risk from sphincterotomy
Conservative and medical therapy (topical diltiazem + stool softeners) strongly preferred in elderly over surgery
Botulinum toxin preferred over surgical LIS in elderly patients with any pre-existing incontinence risk
Medication review: identify and switch constipating medications where possible
Higher prevalence of anal fissures in HIV-positive patients, particularly those with low CD4 counts

Secondary causes extremely important in HIV-positive patients with anal fissure: herpes simplex (very painful; multiple vesicular ulcers); CMV (deep ulcers; painless); syphilis; Kaposi's sarcoma; lymphoma; anal cancer (SCC — 40x higher incidence in HIV-positive MSM)
ALL HIV-positive patients with atypical anal fissures must have: biopsy; full STI screen; colonoscopy if systemic features
Standard fissure treatment principles apply but healing may be slower in immunocompromised
ART (antiretroviral therapy) optimisation to improve CD4 count is the most important intervention for healing
Aciclovir/valaciclovir if HSV proctitis is identified

Crohn's disease causes complex anal fissures — typically: multiple; lateral location; large; undermined edges; painless or minimally painful (paradoxically less painful than primary fissures); associated with skin tags, fistulae, and abscesses
Crohn's anal fissures require colonoscopy for Crohn's assessment and disease staging before treatment

Medical treatment of Crohn's disease (biological therapies — anti-TNF: infliximab, adalimumab; anti-integrin: vedolizumab; Janus kinase inhibitors) often improves anorectal Crohn's fissures significantly — treat the underlying Crohn's before local fissure treatment
Surgical sphincterotomy (LIS) is CONTRAINDICATED in active Crohn's proctitis — very high risk of non-healing and fistula formation
Botulinum toxin may be used cautiously in Crohn's fissures
Metronidazole and ciprofloxacin are adjunct antibiotics for perianal Crohn's disease (reduce perianal sepsis)

vaccinations_recommended.vaccine: HPV Vaccine (Human Papillomavirus) — Prevention of Anal Cancer
vaccinations_recommended.frequency: 2-dose schedule (6-12 months apart) if started before 15 years; 3-dose schedule for 15+ years or immunocompromised
vaccinations_recommended.reason: HPV (particularly types 16 and 18) is the primary cause of anal squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) — the most important differential diagnosis for a non-healing anal ulcer. Anal SCC incidence has increased dramatically in MSM and HIV-positive populations. HPV-related anal fissure-like ulcers and condylomata (anal warts — from HPV 6/11) are important secondary causes of anorectal symptoms. HPV vaccination prevents HPV-associated anal cancer and anal warts. Particularly recommended for: MSM; all adolescents; HIV-positive individuals (up to age 45 in MSM per guidelines); women up to age 26 (standard) or 45 (shared decision); individuals with prior HPV-related lesions.
vaccinations_recommended.who_should_prioritise: MSM; HIV-positive; adolescents (before sexual debut); women with abnormal cervical smear history; any patient with HPV-related anal/perianal lesions

vaccinations_recommended.reason: Influenza causes systemic illness with prolonged immobility and dehydration — both worsen constipation and can precipitate or worsen anal fissure in vulnerable patients. Patients with IBD (Crohn's — a secondary cause of anal fissure) are on immunosuppressive medications (biologicals, corticosteroids, azathioprine) and are at significantly higher risk of severe influenza — annual vaccination is strongly recommended in this group. In the general population with anal fissure, influenza vaccination reduces illness that causes constipation relapse.

Hepatitis A causes GI inflammation with diarrhoea and abdominal cramps — prolonged or severe diarrhoea is a recognised cause of anal fissure (repeated frequent loose stools cause cumulative mucosal trauma). Hepatitis A vaccination is particularly relevant for travellers to endemic areas; patients with IBD (who are more susceptible to GI infections); and healthcare workers. Vaccination prevents hepatitis A-associated diarrhoeal illness that could trigger or worsen anal fissure.

COVID-19 causes GI symptoms (diarrhoea, constipation, GI motility disruption) in 30-40% of cases. The post-COVID period is associated with significant bowel motility changes (constipation or diarrhoea) that can trigger or worsen anal fissure. Patients with IBD (secondary fissure cause) are at higher risk of severe COVID-19 on immunosuppressants. Vaccination protects against COVID-related GI complications and IBD flares triggered by COVID-19.

vaccinations_recommended.vaccine: Typhoid Vaccine (for travellers and endemic area residents)
vaccinations_recommended.frequency: Every 3 years (oral) or single dose (Vi polysaccharide injection)
vaccinations_recommended.reason: Typhoid fever causes severe constipation in the early stages (Peyer's patches involvement → ileal motility disruption) — 'pea-soup diarrhoea' in later stages can also cause anal fissure. In India (endemic country), typhoid is a relevant cause of GI disease; typhoid vaccination prevents typhoid-induced bowel disturbance that can trigger or worsen anal fissure. Particularly relevant for those in high-exposure environments.

Herpes zoster (shingles) can cause sacral nerve root involvement (S2-S4 dermatome — 'perineal shingles') with vesicular eruption in the anal and perineal area — closely mimicking or exacerbating anal fissure; severe sacral herpes zoster causes anal and urinary retention from autonomic involvement. In elderly patients with pre-existing anal fissure, shingles in the sacral dermatome dramatically worsens pain and may trigger severe anal sphincter spasm. Shingrix vaccination prevents shingles and its perianal complications.

when_to_see_doctor: Severe anal pain during and after defecation (lasting more than 30-60 minutes after bowel movement) for more than 1-2 weeks — formal diagnosis and treatment planning needed
Bright red rectal bleeding on toilet paper or dripping into the pan — first presentation always requires clinical assessment to confirm fissure and exclude haemorrhoids or more serious causes
An anal fissure not improving after 4-6 weeks of self-managed conservative treatment (fibre, hydration, warm baths)
Inability to defecate normally due to fear of pain — defecation avoidance behaviour causing progressive constipation
Presence of a visible skin tag (sentinel pile) at the anal verge — suggests chronicity requiring active medical treatment
Visible non-healing ulcer or lump near the anus lasting more than 3-4 weeks — biopsy may be required to exclude anal cancer
Multiple anal fissures, or fissure at an unusual location (lateral — not at 6 or 12 o'clock) — secondary cause investigation required
Anal fissure associated with diarrhoea, weight loss, abdominal pain, or bloody diarrhoea — possible Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis
Post-partum women with severe anal pain on defecation in the first 3 months after delivery — post-partum fissure assessment and safe treatment
Infants and toddlers with bright red blood on nappies or wipes, or who cry during bowel movements — paediatric anal fissure assessment
Patients with HIV, Crohn's disease, or immunosuppression developing anorectal pain or ulceration — secondary causes require prompt assessment
Anal fissure in patients aged >45-50 that fails to respond to standard treatment — mandatory biopsy to exclude anal carcinoma
emergency_signs: Inability to pass urine (urinary retention) combined with severe perianal pain — possible perianal abscess or sacral nerve root involvement — URGENT assessment

Perianal swelling with redness, heat, and throbbing pain (particularly between defecations — not just with defecation) with fever — PERIANAL ABSCESS — requires URGENT surgical drainage within 24-48 hours (may progress to necrotising fasciitis if untreated)

Fever, chills, and severe systemic illness combined with perianal pain — possible spreading perianal sepsis (Fournier's gangrene — rare, life-threatening necrotising fasciitis of the perineum) — CALL EMERGENCY SERVICES IMMEDIATELY

Fournier's Gangrene signs: rapidly spreading perianal swelling; necrotic skin; severe systemic sepsis; crepitus (crackling sensation from gas-producing organisms in tissue) — LIFE-THREATENING EMERGENCY — immediate surgical debridement required
Sudden onset of inability to defecate at all (complete constipation) with severe anal pain and abdominal distension — possible impacted faecal mass with anorectal obstruction — URGENT assessment

Massive rectal bleeding (more than a few drops) — while not typical of simple anal fissure, any significant rectal haemorrhage requires urgent colorectal assessment to exclude haemorrhoidal bleed, diverticular bleed, or colorectal cancer

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is an anal fissure and why is it so painful?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: An anal fissure is a small tear in the lining of the anal canal — the last part of the intestine that opens at the anus. Despite its small size (often just a few millimetres), it causes disproportionately severe pain for two reasons: (1) The anal canal lining is among the most densely innervated tissue in the body — every tiny sensation is sharply felt; (2) The tear triggers a spasm of the internal anal sphincter (the circular muscle around the anal canal) — this spasm is sustained for 1-4 hours after defecation, causing the prolonged burning, throbbing pain. The spasm also reduces blood supply to the area, preventing healing and creating a vicious cycle. The good news: anal fissures are benign and very treatable.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Is the bright red blood from an anal fissure serious?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Bright red blood on toilet paper or dripping into the bowl after defecation from an anal fissure is NOT dangerous or life-threatening in itself. It comes from small blood vessels in the tear and is typically in small amounts. HOWEVER, rectal bleeding always requires a medical assessment — at least once — to confirm it is from a fissure and exclude other causes such as haemorrhoids, polyps, or colorectal cancer. Signs that rectal bleeding needs URGENT assessment: large volumes of blood; blood mixed in stool (not just on the surface); dark red or tarry black blood (melaena); blood with mucus; blood associated with weight loss or change in bowel habit; any rectal bleeding in a patient over 45 years without a clear prior diagnosis. For confirmed small-volume bright red blood in a young patient with the typical fissure pain pattern, conservative treatment is usually first.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Will my anal fissure heal on its own without treatment?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Acute anal fissures (less than 6 weeks old) heal spontaneously in approximately 50% of cases with conservative measures (dietary fibre, adequate water, warm sitz baths, stool softeners) within 6-8 weeks. The key is ensuring soft stools — without soft stools, even spontaneous healing is unlikely. Chronic fissures (present more than 6-8 weeks) have a much lower spontaneous healing rate (<10%) and almost always require active medical treatment (topical GTN or diltiazem cream) or surgical intervention. Starting dietary and conservative measures early dramatically improves the chance of spontaneous healing and preventing chronicity.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is the GTN ointment and how do I use it correctly?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: GTN (glyceryl trinitrate) ointment is a prescription cream that acts as a 'chemical sphincterotomy' — it releases nitric oxide gas that relaxes the internal anal sphincter muscle, reducing the spasm and improving blood flow to allow healing. For best results: (1) Apply a pea-sized amount (about 2-3cm from the tube) to the anal opening only — not to a wide area around it; (2) Use a disposable glove, finger cot, or gauze — NOT your bare finger; (3) Apply twice daily — once in the morning (30 minutes BEFORE your expected bowel movement if possible) and once before bed; (4) Take a paracetamol 30 minutes BEFORE applying to reduce headache; (5) NEVER use if you take Viagra, Cialis, Levitra, or similar medications — dangerous blood pressure drop can occur. Headache is common — reduce to once daily if severe; do not stop without completing 6-8 weeks.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Is topical diltiazem better than GTN for anal fissure?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Both topical diltiazem (2% cream) and GTN (0.2-0.4% ointment) have similar effectiveness for healing chronic anal fissures (approximately 50-65% healing rates). The key difference is tolerability: GTN causes headaches in 20-40% of patients (from nitrate vasodilation) — the most common reason people stop treatment. Diltiazem causes headache in only about 5% and causes only mild perianal irritation in some patients. In practice: try diltiazem first if you are concerned about headaches, if you take Viagra/Cialis (GTN is absolutely contraindicated with these), if you are breastfeeding, or if a previous GTN trial was stopped due to headache. GTN is slightly more widely studied and available. Both work — choose based on your circumstances.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is botulinum toxin (Botox) injection for anal fissure and is it painful?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Botulinum toxin (Botox) injection into the internal anal sphincter is a minimally invasive treatment — usually performed as an outpatient procedure, often with topical or local anaesthetic. A small needle is used to inject 20-40 units of Botox directly into the sphincter muscle. The toxin temporarily paralyses the muscle for about 3-4 months, reducing spasm and allowing the fissure to heal. Healing rate: 50-70% with one injection; up to 80% with two injections. The procedure itself causes brief discomfort during injection — most patients find it much less painful than they expect. The main side effect is temporary minor incontinence (mainly gas/mucus) in 10-20% of patients, which resolves spontaneously as the Botox wears off. It is a good bridge between topical treatment and surgery.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is lateral internal sphincterotomy (LIS) surgery and when is it needed?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Lateral internal sphincterotomy (LIS) is a brief day-case surgical procedure — the gold standard surgical treatment for chronic anal fissure. Under general or spinal anaesthesia, a small incision is made at the side (lateral position) of the anus, and the lower third of the internal sphincter muscle is cut. This permanently reduces the muscle tightness, allowing normal blood flow and healing. It is highly effective — 90-95% of chronic fissures heal after LIS. Surgery is considered when: the fissure is confirmed chronic (>8 weeks) and has failed two courses of topical medical treatment AND botulinum toxin; or when the patient specifically requests definitive treatment. The main risk is faecal incontinence — minor gas or moisture soiling affects about 5-10% of patients. In most, this is temporary and mild. Modern careful surgical technique minimises this risk.

frequently_asked_questions.question: How can I prevent my anal fissure from coming back after it heals?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Recurrence is common (30-50% with medical treatment; 5-10% with surgery) — almost always from return of constipation and hard stools. Prevention strategies: (1) Permanently maintain a high-fibre diet (25-35g/day) — daily dal, whole grains, sabzi, fruits; (2) Continue Isabgol or other fibre supplement indefinitely if needed; (3) Stay well hydrated (2 litres daily); (4) Respond promptly to any constipation — do not let hard stools return; (5) Use a footstool under feet when on the toilet — reduces straining; (6) Never suppress the urge to defecate — go when you feel the need; (7) Continue warm sitz baths periodically even after healing — good anal hygiene and circulation; (8) Avoid constipating medications (opioids, iron supplements) as much as possible — speak to your doctor about alternatives; (9) If constipation returns — restart stool softeners immediately and see your doctor if it persists >1 week.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What foods should I eat and avoid with anal fissure?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: EAT MORE: High-fibre whole grains (bajra, jowar, ragi, whole wheat chapati, brown rice); daily dal and legumes (masoor dal, chana, rajma); plenty of vegetables especially pumpkin (kaddu), bottle gourd (lauki), okra (bhindi), spinach (cooked), and leafy greens; fruits especially papaya (daily — excellent for gut motility), guava, pear with skin, apple with skin, prunes and anjeer; 2-2.5 litres of water daily; buttermilk (chaach) and curd (probiotics); 1-2 teaspoons Isabgol in water if needed. AVOID OR REDUCE: White rice and white maida as main diet (replace with whole grains); spicy hot food (irritates fissure wound on passing); alcohol; excessive caffeine without water; constipating foods (unripe bananas, excess cheese, processed foods). The single most impactful change: eat papaya daily + drink 2 litres water + use Isabgol if needed = significantly softer stools.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Is it true that squatting on the toilet is better than sitting for anal fissure?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Yes — this is well-supported by physiology. The 'squatting position' (feet on the floor with knees raised above hip level) aligns the anorectal angle more favourably for defecation: the puborectalis muscle (which maintains the 90-degree anorectal angle when standing) relaxes in the squatting position, allowing the anal canal to straighten. This means stool passes with significantly less required straining effort. Most Indian and Asian traditional toilets (Indian squatting pans) provide this position naturally. On a Western-style toilet: placing a small stool (20-25cm height — the 'Squatty Potty' device or a plastic step stool) under your feet achieves the same effect. A study in Diseases of the Colon and Rectum showed squatting reduced defecation time by 50% and eliminated straining in most subjects. For anal fissure patients specifically: less straining = less mechanical stress on the fissure = faster healing.

frequently_asked_questions.question: My doctor said my anal fissure might be related to Crohn's disease. What does that mean?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Anal fissures usually occur at the posterior midline (6 o'clock position) and are exquisitely painful. When a fissure is: at an unusual position (the sides — lateral), multiple, large, relatively painless, or associated with anal skin tags, fistulae, or bowel symptoms (diarrhoea, weight loss, blood in stool, abdominal pain) — Crohn's disease must be excluded. Crohn's disease is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease that can affect the anus and perianal area, causing complex fissures, fistulae, and abscesses. If Crohn's is suspected, a colonoscopy will be arranged. Crohn's-related anal fissures are treated differently from primary fissures — treating the underlying Crohn's inflammation (with biological drugs like infliximab or adalimumab) often heals the perianal fissure; surgical sphincterotomy is generally avoided in active Crohn's proctitis as healing is impaired. The most important message: any atypical fissure needs proper evaluation before assuming it is a simple primary fissure.
